title: Two places, one James?
standfirst: Six indexed baptisms name James Glasgow in two parishes. The original 1605 Mid Calder page adds a probable Murieston residence and witness George Glasgow, possibly the man named there in 1586. The cross-parish identity and older kinship remain open.
question: Do the Mid Calder and Inveresk baptisms belong to the same James?
answer: Mid Calder indexes name a father James in 1605, 1610 and 1616, while Inveresk/Musselburgh indexes do so in 1609, 1614 and 1618. Andrew of Calder's corrected testament names no son James, so it cannot establish James's parentage. The children must not be moved, split or merged on name and locality alone.

chapters.title: The Duddingston weaver branch: retain the stronger father link
body: James Glasgow-1150 remains probably the son of Robert Glasgow-1156: the existing apprentice, burgess and Duddingston burial comparison retains its grade. The 17 October review changes the preferred parents above Robert to Andrew Glasgow-3163 and Elizat Stevinsoun-2, both uncertain through possible identity with their testament-named son Robert Glasgow-4006. This affects the 64-profile pre-1850 child side without making the later Robert identity or his adult parentage certain. The earlier Archibald Glasgow-1097 and Isobell Newlands-647 parents remain unselected alternatives. The two Robert profiles remain separate.

The accepted 1597/8 testament directly documents Andrew, wife Elizat and son Robert; Elizat’s record-defined maternity and the spouse relationship are now formally graded documented. The son’s already-confident father is reaffirmed. The original clause is reused from the accepted illustrated reading, not newly inspected. No live WikiTree parent, vital field or certainty flag changed.

chapters.title: Murieston: George’s 1586–1605 identity is probable
body: The preferred working identification is that George Glasgw in Mureistoun in the 1586 Calder muster obligation was the adult George Glasgow who witnessed the 17 February 1605 baptism of George, son of James Glasgow in provisionally read Muirestoun. The 1605 household points to the same holding as the earlier George, within the same parish setting. The surname is specific to this local comparison, and a 19-year interval is straightforward for one adult career. A child bearing George’s name and an adult George participating in his baptism make a continuing local family association more economical than two unconnected Georges. Together these observations warrant probable rather than merely possible cross-record identity. They do not amount to independent proofs of every step.

The witness’s own residence is unstated, and another George in the district remains possible. The residence reading Muirestoun and its identification as Murieston remain probable. Shared spelling and locality are related observations; McCall repeats Maidment’s 1586 act and is not a second muster occurrence. Naming the child George is supporting context, not proof of a naming rule. The 1586 act records an obligation, not attendance. Neither source gives George’s age or states a relationship to James. Father, uncle, brother, other kinsman and neighbour remain alternatives. No father is changed: Andrew Glasgow-3163 remains James’s selected uncertain father, while George is an important competing paternal or collateral explanation. George Glasgow-1099, the merchant, remains compatible but unselected; the 1586 minor’s curatorship and the 1598 marriage contract do not identify him at Murieston. No mother, birth date, identity merge or confidently marked paternal edge is added.

This improves a specific identity assessment within the 216-profile James branch, rather than raising Andrew’s father grade. The earlier possible assessment is retained as history. The working tree, confident paternal graph and fixed cohort are unchanged. The underlying 1605 register page was freshly inspected for this review; the 1586 printed-page verification from 15 October is retained, and the court manuscript remains unread.

chapters.title: Four selected working connections
body: The local working tree now selects Andrew of Calder as tentative father of James, John of Linlithgow and David of Mid Calder. It selects the older Mid Calder/Quothquan John as tentative father of the1640s Kirknewton John. These are logical reconstructions from material already on this site, not newly discovered parentage records.

James Glasgow → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: Andrew’s documented rural Calder household is the preferred working anchor for James’s nearby Mid Calder family. He was alive across the estimated1575–1586 birth interval of all three Lothian fathers; Hermand John’s1577 death would require an earlier birth estimate for David. That favours this coherent provisional family without excluding the other father. Andrew was alive until1598 and the uncertain generations allow James to be an older son. This uses the actual Calder setting and compatible family sequence, not the withdrawn assertion that the testament named James. James’s Inveresk/Fisherrow identity remains a separate uncertainty. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 is another plausible older local father. The George named at Mureistoun1586 and the George witness1605 are a competing father/relative lead; identifying that George with merchant1099 would require additional identity assumptions and young fatherhood. None is excluded. Andrew’s omission of James weakens this model; it does not disprove an older son.

John Glasgow of Linlithgow → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: Select the same older Calder household as the working origin for this neighbouring Lothian family. John’s estimated1579 generation and children recorded1613–1622 fit an older son of Andrew, whose own father is tentatively John-1093. The proximity and compatible generations make this a useful shared-family model alongside James and David, rather than an assertion that the three are proved brothers. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 is a compatible alternative if John1561’s estimated birth is earlier than1577. A separate unnamed local father remains possible. Andrew’s1598 testament does not name John; do not restore the obsolete James/Andrew/William child list or attach Jonet Anderson as mother.

David Glasgow of Mid Calder → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: David’s1606 and1612 Mid Calder baptisms place his household in the same small Calder area as the earlier Andrew household. His approximate generation permits Andrew to be his father. The first recorded daughter Elspeth is consistent with the Elizat name in Andrew’s household, a minor naming clue rather than a mother identification. Select Andrew as the tentative shared father with James and John; exact birth years remain estimates. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 or another older local Glasgow could be the father. If David’s approximate1586 birth were established, he would have been young when omitted from Andrew’s1598 testament, making that omission more troublesome. It is not an established birth date. Elizat Stevinsoun and the discredited Jonet Anderson attribution are not automatically assigned as mothers.

John Glasgow of Kirknewton → John Glasgow, Mid Calder/Quothquan working identity: The older John already represents the father named in Mid Calder baptisms1608–1609. His son John-1086, baptised1608, is a viable earlier identity for the adult John who had children in neighbouring Kirknewton/East Calder1646–1650: age38 at the1646 birth is straightforward. Select the older John as working father of3610 on that local and chronological reconstruction. Keep the two son profiles separate while testing their possible identity. Alternatives: John-1086 has a later Biggar account that has not been equated with3610. They may be different men, and the older father’s Mid Calder/Montfoid/Quothquan identity is itself uncertain. Robert-4006 is another generationally compatible Calder father. This does not restore the former unsupported William-1087 father or treat1629 as a recorded birthday.
All four edges are uncertain and count only in the working pedigree. Confident relationships, raw WikiTree parent fields and the fixed cohort are unchanged. No mother is assigned by these selections.

chapters.title: A corrected parentage boundary
body: Andrew's testament names Robert and three daughters, not James.
It therefore removes a former claimed parentage but does not prove that the two baptism sequences belong to different men.

chapters.title: The Mid Calder sequence
body: Indexes for George, Beatrix and John consistently give their father's forename as James Glasgow.
The original1605 page adds a provisional Muirestoun residence and adult witness George Glasgow; it does not identify James across parishes.

chapters.title: The Inveresk and Musselburgh sequence
body: Indexes for Eduard, William and Agnes likewise name father James Glasgow.
Without occupations, witnesses, a spouse, property or testament evidence, the overlap with Mid Calder remains an open test.

chapters.title: Fisherrow sasine index follow-up (15 October 2026)
body: The reported 1624–25 Fisherrow sasine index identifies a tailor James Glasgow, his spouse Christina Bye and son Alexander; a separate entry identifies Janet Clerk as Alexander’s spouse. Existing James Glasgow-991, Christina Bie-55 and Alexander Glasgow-1148 are compatible candidates.

The printed index and column pairings remain uninspected in the original sasines. The 1614 mother name cited in Glasgow-3517’s live profile has not been verified in the original; fresh Findmypast record R_686177762 names William Glasgow in 1614 with father James but gives no mother or exact day. No cross-parish or parent-certainty upgrade is made.
